title: Mental Status Examination (MSE)
summary: Performing a systematic mental status examination to assess psychiatric and cognitive functioning.
steps: Establish rapport. Ensure privacy and minimize distractions.
APPEARANCE: grooming, hygiene, dress (appropriate to season/weather?), eye contact, psychomotor activity (agitation, retardation).
BEHAVIOR: calm, cooperative, guarded, hostile, bizarre? Level of engagement.
SPEECH: rate (rapid, slow), volume, tone, clarity, quantity (verbose vs. minimal), spontaneous or requires prompting.
MOOD: subjective report from patient in their own words (e.g., 'I feel empty').
AFFECT: objective observed emotional tone. Range (full vs. restricted/blunted/flat), appropriateness to content (congruent vs. incongruent), lability.
THOUGHT PROCESS: logical and linear vs. tangential, circumstantial, flight of ideas, loosening of associations, word salad.
THOUGHT CONTENT: delusions (fixed false beliefs), paranoia, ideas of reference, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation.
PERCEPTIONS: hallucinations (auditory, visual, tactile, olfactory), illusions.
COGNITION: orientation ×4 (person, place, time, situation), memory (recent and remote), attention/concentration (serial 7s), abstract thinking (proverb interpretation).
INSIGHT: does patient understand they have a mental illness and need treatment? (poor, limited, fair, full)
JUDGMENT: hypothetical scenarios (what would you do if you found a stamped envelope?).
safetyTips: Never conduct MSE through a locked door or in a punitive manner — therapeutic alliance affects validity.
SI/HI assessment is part of thought content — always ask directly. Asking about suicide does not increase risk.
Compare findings to baseline and prior documentation.
keyTakeaways: MSE documents objective and subjective psychiatric findings
Mood = subjective (patient words); Affect = objective (nurse observes)

title: Suicide Risk Assessment (Columbia Protocol / C-SSRS)
summary: Assessing suicide ideation and risk using the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS).
equipment: C-SSRS or facility suicide screening tool
steps: Ask ALL patients on admission and per protocol. Do NOT avoid the question — asking does not plant the idea.
C-SSRS IDEATION SCALE:
1. Passive ideation: 'I wish I were dead.' (no intent or plan)
2. Active ideation, no plan, no intent.
3. Active ideation with some method (but no plan or intent).
4. Active ideation with intent but no plan.
5. Active ideation with intent AND plan.
ASSESS ADDITIONAL RISK FACTORS: prior attempts (strongest predictor), means access (gun in home), substance use, recent loss, isolation, hopelessness.
PROTECTIVE FACTORS: social support, religious beliefs, children, reasons for living, engaged in treatment.
LEVEL OF CARE based on findings:
Passive ideation or C-SSRS 1–2: safety plan, follow-up.
Active ideation C-SSRS 3–4: notify provider, consider 1:1 monitoring.
C-SSRS 5 or imminent risk: 1:1 constant observation, STAT psychiatric evaluation, remove means.
Implement environmental safety: remove sharps, ligature points, medications, cords from room.
Document: exact language patient used, C-SSRS score, risk level, actions taken, and provider notification.
safetyTips: Never leave a high-risk patient alone to 'get help' — call from the room or have a colleague come to you.
Removal of means is a proven life-saving intervention. Check the room for sharps, cords, and medications.
Documentation must include exact patient statements — never paraphrase SI/HI as 'denies.'
documentation: C-SSRS score or facility tool result
keyTakeaways: Ask directly — does not increase risk
Prior attempt is the strongest predictor

title: Verbal De-Escalation Techniques
summary: Using evidence-based verbal techniques to reduce agitation and prevent escalation to aggression.
equipment: No physical equipment — your presence, voice, and nonverbal communication
steps: SAFETY FIRST: assess your exit. Do not allow patient to block your egress. Stay near the door.
APPROACH: calm body language. Do NOT cross your arms or point. Maintain non-threatening posture at a slight angle (not directly facing — can feel confrontational).
PERSONAL SPACE: allow extra space (1.5–3× normal) for agitated patients. Approaching too close escalates.
VOICE: calm, quiet, slow. Lower volume often has more effect than raising it.
LISTEN: allow patient to express grievances without interruption. Use reflective listening: 'It sounds like you're feeling frustrated because...'
VALIDATE the emotion without necessarily agreeing with behavior: 'I can see why that would be upsetting.'
OFFER CHOICES to restore a sense of control: 'Would you like to talk here or in the quiet room?'
AVOID: arguing, threatening, authoritative posturing, sarcasm, or telling patient to 'calm down.'
SET LIMITS CLEARLY and calmly: 'I need you to lower your voice so we can talk about this.'
TEAM RESPONSE: if escalating, call for a show of force calmly — additional staff present without threatening.
LAST RESORT: chemical or physical restraint per facility policy and provider order.
safetyTips: Your safety is the priority. No intervention is worth a physical assault.
Never touch an agitated patient without warning — it can trigger physical aggression.
Document all de-escalation attempts before using restraints.

title: Therapeutic Communication Skills
summary: Applying therapeutic communication techniques to establish trust and facilitate patient disclosure.
equipment: No equipment — requires skill and presence
steps: ACTIVE LISTENING: give full attention. Make eye contact. Nod. Avoid interrupting or finishing the patient's sentences.
OPEN-ENDED QUESTIONS: 'Tell me more about that' rather than yes/no questions.
FOCUSING: bring patient back to key theme: 'You mentioned earlier that you were feeling hopeless — can you tell me more about that?'
REFLECTION: mirror back feelings or content: 'It sounds like you felt abandoned by your family.'
CLARIFICATION: 'I want to make sure I understand — can you say more about what you mean by that?'
SILENCE: allow therapeutic silence. Do NOT rush to fill silence — it gives the patient time to process and speak.
SUMMARIZING: at end of interaction, summarize key points to validate and confirm understanding.
NONVERBAL SKILLS: lean slightly forward, uncrossed arms, appropriate distance (1.5–3 feet), be at eye level.
AVOID:
Giving advice or false reassurance: 'Everything will be fine.'
Asking 'why' questions (implies judgment): 'Why did you stop your meds?'
Changing the subject when patient discloses something difficult.
Defending the healthcare system or minimizing the patient's concerns.
safetyTips: False reassurance damages trust and discourages future disclosure.
Breaching confidentiality without cause destroys therapeutic alliance — disclose only as required (safety exceptions).
Your reaction to what the patient says will either open or close further communication.
keyTakeaways: Silence is therapeutic — do not rush to fill it

title: Inpatient Behavioral Safety Monitoring (1:1 / Q15)
summary: Conducting structured safety checks for patients on psychiatric observation precautions.
steps: Determine level of observation ordered by provider:
Q15 (every 15 minutes): high-risk patient not requiring constant observation.
1:1 constant: patient in sight at all times. Staff within arm's reach.
1:1 direct: maximum risk. Staff within arm's reach AT ALL TIMES (including bathroom).
Q15 CHECKS: at each 15-minute interval, visually locate patient and document: location, behavior (sleeping, talking, calm, agitated), and physical status.
STAGGER the checks — do NOT do them at exactly 15:00, 15:15, 15:30 (patients learn the pattern). Vary slightly within each window.
1:1 CONSTANT: staff must maintain visual contact at ALL times. Cannot leave to get supplies. Must be relieved for breaks.
Environmental safety check each shift: scan room for ligature points, weapons, accumulated medications, sharps, and hazardous items.
Document each check accurately. False documentation (noting patient as calm when not observed) is a serious safety and legal issue.
Report any concerns immediately to charge nurse/provider.
safetyTips: Never falsify observation records. Documenting without actually observing has led to patient suicides and criminal charges against nurses.
Patients on 1:1 constant must be visible during bathroom use (door ajar or female staff present per policy).
If the patient refuses to be seen, this must be documented AND reported to the charge nurse — it is a safety event.
documentation: Behavior and status at each check
keyTakeaways: Stagger Q15 checks to prevent predictability
False documentation is a criminal matter
